title: Replacing a leather writing surface on a writing desk
subtitle: Remove the old leather inset from a writing desk lid or top, clean the recess, cut new leather to fit, and glue it in with a smooth finish and tooled border
excerpt: How to replace a worn leather writing surface on a writing desk or bureau. Covers removing the old leather, measuring and cutting the new panel, applying adhesive, and fitting the tooled or plain border edge.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced). UK furniture restoration trade practice. Bookbinding and desk restoration guides (public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: The thin split-grain sheep or goat leather (typically 0.4 to 0.8 mm thick) used as the inset writing surface on a writing desk, bureau, or library table. Mounted in a recessed panel. Available in a range of marbled, plain, and hand-tooled colours from bookbinding and restoration suppliers.

A traditional wheat-starch and hide-glue paste used in bookbinding and desk restoration to bond leather to a surface. Dries slowly, allowing the leather to be repositioned. The correct adhesive for desk skivers; PVA is also acceptable but sets faster and allows less adjustment.

content.text: A writing desk's leather surface is a
glued into a recessed panel. When it splits, wears through, or peels, the replacement job is: strip the old leather cleanly, measure precisely, cut the new panel to fit, and glue with
or PVA. The finish quality depends on the cutting precision and the flatness of the glue-down.

Lift a corner of the old leather with a filling knife. Work the knife under the leather and peel back slowly. If the leather is well-adhered, dampen the surface very lightly with water and leave for a few minutes to soften the old glue before peeling. Scrape all the old glue residue from the recess with the filling knife. The recess surface must be flat and clean before the new leather goes down.

Measure the length and width of the recess at several points; old desk recesses are rarely perfectly square. Cut a paper template first and test the fit before cutting the leather. The paper must sit flat in the recess with the corners touching without curling. Transfer the paper template onto the new skiver and cut with the leatherwork knife against a steel rule.
Apply the adhesive and fit the skiver

Apply a thin, even coat of hide paste or a dilute PVA (1:1 PVA to water) to the recess surface. Let it become almost dry and slightly tacky. Position the skiver carefully in the recess: grain side up, one long edge placed first, then smoothed flat with a clean cloth or a roller working from the centre out toward the edges. Press firmly into the corners. Work out any air bubbles immediately. Place a flat board with heavy weights on top and leave for at least 3 hours.
Trim the edges and add a border

Once the glue has set, trim any overlap at the recess edges with the leatherwork knife held vertically against the wall. The cut edge should meet the recess wall cleanly. For a traditional finish, run a brass finishing fillet (a ruling wheel) along the border to stamp a gold or blind line. These tools come from bookbinding suppliers.

attrs.symptom: Skiver bubbles or lifts at the centre after the weights are removed
attrs.cause: Air was trapped under the leather during gluing, or the adhesive dried too quickly.
attrs.fix: Carefully lift the bubbled section, apply more adhesive to the recess and the leather back, then smooth flat again and weight.

attrs.symptom: The new leather wrinkles at the corners of the recess
attrs.cause: The paper template was not tested first and the leather cut slightly too large.
attrs.fix: Remove the leather while the adhesive is still soft. Trim 1 mm from the relevant edges, then refit.
